stories.title: 'High risk' of lake bursting and causing second flood, warns China
stories.summary: China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst, causing a second flood downstream. The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river. As of Friday morning, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated at the barrier lake, according to state broadcaster CCTV. A barrier lake is a body of water formed when debris dams up a river. Officials said that three million cubic metres of water is expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and Saturday, posing a "high risk of breach". The barrier lake, which formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, has already started to overflow, according to China's Ministry of Water Resources. The area has also seen heavy rain. Authorities have sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions. A CCTV report on Friday morning said that most of the Chinese emergency services were stuck at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood. This was because the barrier lake was "overflowing non-stop" which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows. Due to the risks, search and rescue operations had to be suspended near the Nepal-Tibet border, according to the report. The lake is in the same region as the Langtang Lirung peak, where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port.

stories.title: Japan Airlines to introduce aircraft-washing robot at airport near Tokyo
stories.summary: The AW3 robot can clean an aircraft using a remotely operated telescopic arm.
article_sentences: Japan Airlines (JAL) said on Aug 28 that it will introduce a robot that washes aircraft exteriors at Narita airport, near Tokyo, the first to do so among domestic airlines.

The AW3 robot, developed by Sweden-based Aerowash, can clean an aircraft using a remotely operated telescopic arm and will start full-scale operation later in 2026, after staff complete necessary training, the airline said.
The airline said some manual cleaning will continue with long-handled mops but that is expects labour hours to be reduced by up to 40 per cent per aircraft.
Apart from reducing workloads, automation will reduce the risk to staff of working at heights and exposure to chemicals, it said.

JAL held a demonstration for the press at its aircraft washing facility at Narita airport in Chiba prefecture on Aug 28, showcasing both the current manual washing method and the automated washing method using the AW3.

Atsuki Kino of JAL’s Airport Ground Handling Planning Department said: “The goal is not to reduce staff, but to reduce their workloads so they can use the time saved to perform other high-value tasks, changing the way they work.”

stories.title: Will Australia be locked out of top scientific research by shunning Chinese universities?
stories.summary: Australia’s decision to axe partnerships with two Chinese universities has raised concerns that Canberra is moving to align with Washington on research security policy. The decision came after the United States expanded its restrictions on research entities from China. One analyst warned that Canberra’s latest move would not hinder Chinese progress, but it could leave Australia locked out of top-tier scientific research. stories.title: Bank holiday weekend to see more thunderstorms and rain
stories.summary: Most of the UK is finally getting some rain, in time for the bank holiday weekend. The weather will remain unsettled across the next few days with showers, longer spells of rain and thunderstorms all likely at times. By Monday the focus of the wet weather is likely to be across Scotland, with sunny spells developing elsewhere. The RAC estimates that 20 million trips by car will be made across the weekend in what could be challenging driving conditions. Showers and longer spells of rain will continue to affect the UK on Friday, with heavy downpours and thunderstorms possible, especially across western Scotland, Wales and north-west England. Some of this wet weather could spread east later, with thunderstorms possible across north-east England and eastern Scotland. After the recent warm and humid conditions, temperatures by Friday will feel fresher. Expect around 20–23C (68 -73F) in England and Wales, and 16–20C (61-68F) in Scotland and Northern Ireland. These temperatures are around average for late August. Saturday will remain unsettled, with sunny spells mixed with heavy showers and possible thunderstorms, particularly across England and Wales. Fresh westerly winds will make it feel blustery, with highs of 18-22C (64-72F) in England and Wales and 16-19C (61-66F) further north. Sunday and Bank Holiday Monday - for England and Wales - will stay changeable, with further heavy showers, longer spells of rain and a risk of thunderstorms once again.

stories.title: Japan’s education ministry creates guidelines to help schools deal with overbearing parents
stories.summary: The guidelines provide examples of how schools should handle such situations.
article_sentences: Japan's education ministry has created guidelines to help schools handle verbal abuse and unreasonable demands from overbearing parents.
The guidelines advise schools to record interactions, involve multiple staff, and firmly address behaviour that is socially unacceptable.
A 2025 survey revealed 40% of schools face excessive complaints, with many teachers finding dealing with parents burdensome, prompting use of legal support and dedicated staff.

The education ministry has compiled guidelines to help schools prevent or deal with instances of teachers being subjected to verbal abuse, unreasonable demands and other forms of harassment by students’ parents or guardians.
The guidelines, which will soon be provided to boards of education and other entities nationwide, provide examples of how schools should handle such situations.
These include recording interactions with parents who repeatedly and persistently make demands of teachers, and having multiple teachers deal with overbearing parents.
The revised comprehensive promotion of labour measures law, which will take effect from October, mandates customer harassment prevention measures for companies and other entities.
Under the amended law, boards of education and incorporated educational institutions also will be obligated to take steps to prevent such harassment against teachers.
The guidelines drawn up by the Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Ministry clarify schools’ responsibilities and criteria for judging the behaviour of parents under the law.

The guidelines state that parents and residents are partners who support the growth and development of students, and that a school must seriously address any opinions, requests and inquiries directed to it.
Nevertheless, to protect the children and teachers, the guidelines state that schools must take a firm stand against any behaviour that “goes beyond what is socially acceptable”.

Examples of unacceptable behavior include unreasonably demanding a child be put in another class or get a different homeroom teacher; demanding teachers supervise children playing at a park; staying on the school premises for a long time; and frequently making long phone calls to the school.
